recipes.name: 57 Chevy with a White License Plate

facts.context: Beer volume; revised prior-year baseline. Not pure alcohol.
facts.fact: Kirin estimates that the world consumed 194.12 billion litres of beer in 2024, up 0.5% on its revised 2023 figure.
facts.hook: 194 billion litres. Give or take.

facts.context: Total volume, not consumption per person.
facts.fact: China led total beer consumption for the 22nd consecutive year in 2024, even as its volume fell 3.7%.
facts.hook: Biggest crowd. Different winner.

facts.context: Population average; not an average drinker's intake.
facts.fact: Czechia's 2024 beer consumption was 148.8 litres per resident, the highest per-capita figure for the 32nd consecutive year.
facts.hook: The Czech round is a different size.

facts.context: Year-on-year beer volume; top-25 comparison only.
facts.fact: India's beer consumption rose 14.6% in 2024, the fastest growth among Kirin's top 25 beer-consuming countries.
facts.hook: India's next round is growing.

facts.context: Regional volume share.
facts.fact: Asia accounted for 32.6% of global beer consumption in 2024, remaining the largest consuming region for the 17th year running.
facts.hook: A third of the beer is over here.

facts.context: Estimate; one hectolitre equals 100 litres.
facts.fact: OIV estimates global wine consumption at 208 million hectolitres in 2025, down 2.7% from 2024.
facts.hook: Wine is having a quieter year.

facts.context: Production is not consumption; industrial uses also matter.
facts.fact: World wine production was estimated at 227 million hectolitres in 2025: a 0.6% rebound, but a third consecutive comparatively low vintage.
facts.hook: The vintage stayed small.

facts.context: All vineyard area in OIV's measure; not only wine-grape plots.
facts.fact: Global vineyard area fell to 7.0 million hectares in 2025, down 0.8%, its sixth consecutive annual decline.
facts.hook: Even the vineyard map is shrinking.

facts.context: Export value, not retail spending.
facts.fact: Global wine exports reached 94.8 million hectolitres and €33.8 billion in 2025; volume fell 4.7% and value 6.7%.
facts.hook: A well-travelled bottle.

facts.context: Exports and equivalent bottles; rounded figures.
facts.fact: Scotch exports were worth £5.3 billion in 2025. The SWA reports about 1.34 billion 70 cl bottle equivalents, or 43 per second.
facts.hook: Scotland ships 43 a second.

facts.context: Scotch export volume, not all whisky sold or consumed in India.
facts.fact: India was Scotch's largest export destination by volume in 2025: 220 million 70 cl bottle equivalents, up 15%.
facts.hook: India leads this queue.

facts.context: Export value; different from volume leadership.
facts.fact: The United States was Scotch's biggest export market by value in 2025, at £933 million, versus India's £286 million.
facts.hook: America picks up the larger bill.

facts.context: U.S. adult self-report, not a global consumption measure.
facts.fact: In Gallup's 2025 poll, 54% of U.S. adults said they drank alcohol, down from 62% in 2023 and 58% in 2024.
facts.hook: The room is drinking less.

facts.context: The first figure is an estimate; the second is a forecast, not a result.
facts.fact: IWSR estimated no-alcohol analogue volumes grew 9% in 2025 and forecast 36% growth between 2024 and 2029.
facts.hook: The zero-proof shelf has momentum.

facts.context: Changing panel of 100 award-winning bars; not worldwide unit sales.
facts.fact: The Negroni ranked first in Drinks International's 2026 classic-cocktail report, its fifth consecutive year at number one.
facts.hook: Still ordering the usual?

facts.context: The same bar survey as F015; treat as one shared dataset.
facts.fact: The Margarita was second and the Old Fashioned third in the 2026 report, reversing their long-established order behind the Negroni.
facts.hook: The Margarita moved up a seat.

facts.context: Study conditions included beer at 6°C; glass cavities change the estimate.
facts.fact: A 2021 model estimated roughly 200,000 to nearly two million bubbles could form before a 250 ml lager went flat.
facts.hook: A small beer. A million exits.

facts.context: Approximate pressure; temperature and bottle conditions matter.
facts.fact: A Champagne bottle is typically under about 5–6 bar of pressure.
facts.hook: That cork has pressure behind it.

facts.context: Based on comparative pouring experiments; no universal percentage promised.
facts.fact: Champagne poured down the side of a tilted glass loses less dissolved CO₂ during pouring than a central, upright pour.
facts.hook: The angle changes the fizz.

facts.context: The Marangoni effect; this mechanism is not a wine-quality score.
facts.fact: Wine tears form when evaporation creates surface-tension gradients that drive liquid up the glass; the accumulating ridge then sheds droplets.
facts.hook: The legs are doing physics.

facts.context: Fluorescence, not evidence that the gin itself glows.
facts.fact: Quinine in tonic water fluoresces blue under ultraviolet light.
facts.hook: Your tonic has a second colour.

facts.context: A change in solubility and dispersion; not newly formed crystals.
facts.fact: Diluting anise spirits can make dissolved anethole form tiny oil droplets, turning the drink cloudy: the ouzo effect.
facts.hook: Clear spirit. Cloudy intentions.

facts.context: A 2017 model of one aroma compound, not proof of one ideal dilution for every whisky.
facts.fact: A molecular-simulation study found dilution can move whisky's guaiacol aroma molecule toward the liquid–air interface.
facts.hook: Water changes more than the strength.

facts.context: The downward motion is carried by the liquid; buoyancy has not reversed.
facts.fact: Small bubbles can travel downward near the side of a poured Guinness as rising bubbles drive a circulating liquid flow.
facts.hook: Some bubbles take the stairs down.

facts.context: Brown glass offers more protection than clear or green glass; opaque cans block light.
facts.fact: Light can trigger reactions involving hop-derived iso-alpha acids that produce the potent skunky compound 3-methyl-2-butene-1-thiol.
facts.hook: Sunlight can skunk your beer.

facts.context: Specific panel and test media; not a universal 20% prevalence estimate.
facts.fact: A 2008 study identified rotundone's pepper aroma at a 16 ng/l threshold in red wine; about 20% of its panel could not detect even 4,000 ng/l in water.
facts.hook: That pepper note isn't imaginary.

facts.context: One sensory experiment; screwcaps don't guarantee freedom from TCA.
facts.fact: AWRI found TCA could suppress fruit aroma at 1 ng/l in a Semillon; TCA can also originate from oak and winery contamination.
facts.hook: Cork taint can arrive without a cork.

facts.context: A mechanism relevant to taste, not a guarantee every warming cocktail tastes sweeter.
facts.fact: A 2005 study found the sweet-taste channel TRPM5 strongly temperature-sensitive between 15 and 35°C, with corresponding sweet-response effects in mice.
facts.hook: Temperature is an ingredient.

facts.context: A controlled expectation study; examples included the same wine labelled $5 and $45.
facts.fact: In a 2008 experiment, identical wine presented with a higher price produced higher pleasantness ratings and altered activity in a brain region associated with pleasantness.
facts.hook: Sometimes you're tasting the price tag.

facts.context: An odour-description task, not proof that expertise is worthless.
facts.fact: In a 2001 experiment, 54 tasters described white wine coloured red with red-wine-associated smell vocabulary.
facts.hook: Your eyes get the first sip.

facts.context: Tastings, not 6,000 people. An association in this sample, not a verdict on every expensive wine.
facts.fact: Across more than 6,000 blind tastings, a 2008 study found a small negative price–rating relationship overall; trained tasters showed a different pattern.
facts.hook: Expensive isn't a flavour.

facts.context: Boiling changes alpha acids into bitter iso-alpha acids.
facts.fact: Hops contribute both aroma and bitterness, but different compounds do the work: aromatic oils and bittering acids aren't interchangeable.
facts.hook: Hops have more than one job.

facts.context: Minimum identity requirements, not a quality ranking.
facts.fact: Scotch must be distilled and matured in Scotland for at least three years and bottled at no less than 40% ABV.
facts.hook: Scotch has a minimum age.

facts.context: 'Single malt' does not mean one barrel or one vintage.
facts.fact: Single Malt Scotch comes from one distillery, uses malted barley without other cereals, and is batch-distilled in pot stills.
facts.hook: Single means one distillery.

facts.context: A hypothetical blend of 8-, 12- and 20-year-old whisky is labelled 8 years old.
facts.fact: A Scotch age statement refers to the youngest whisky in the bottle, not the average or the oldest component.
facts.hook: The youngest one gets the label.

facts.context: Kentucky is not mandatory. This is a summary, not the complete production standard.
facts.fact: U.S. rules require bourbon to be distilled and aged in the United States, with at least 51% corn in its mash and new charred oak storage.
facts.hook: Bourbon isn't a Kentucky postcode.

facts.context: Other bourbon production and labelling requirements still apply.
facts.fact: Straight bourbon must spend at least two years in new charred oak; ordinary bourbon has no equivalent two-year minimum.
facts.hook: Straight adds time.

facts.context: Percentages describe fermentable sugars, not the percentage of alcohol in the bottle.
facts.fact: CRT distinguishes '100% agave' tequila from tequila made with at least 51% blue-agave sugars, with other permitted sugars making up the balance.
facts.hook: Tequila has two sugar categories.

facts.context: Maturation class and the 100%-agave category are separate dimensions.
facts.fact: Tequila's minimum oak-contact periods are two months for reposado, one year for añejo and three years for extra añejo.
facts.hook: A little Spanish. A lot of time.

facts.context: An age floor, not the average age or a promise of personal preference.
facts.fact: Cognac's minimum ages are VS: 2 years, VSOP: 4, XO: 10 and XXO: 14, referring to the youngest eau-de-vie in a blend.
facts.hook: Those initials keep time.

facts.context: Do not confuse a style name with a geographical indication.
facts.fact: London gin is a production style and can be made outside London.
facts.hook: London Dry can leave London.

facts.context: Botanical recipes vary; juniper is the common reference point.
facts.fact: Juniper is the defining botanical shared by gin styles, even when citrus, herbs and spices change the rest of the flavour profile.
facts.hook: The berry is the common thread.

facts.context: These are Champagne category thresholds, not universal rules for every wine.
facts.fact: Champagne labelled Extra Dry contains 12–17 g/l of sugar; Brut is below 12 g/l.
facts.hook: Extra Dry is the sweeter answer.

facts.context: It describes the grape source; the wine can still look white.
facts.fact: Blanc de Noirs Champagne is made exclusively from dark-skinned grapes such as Pinot Noir and/or Meunier.
facts.hook: White wine. Dark grapes.

facts.context: Lower numbers mean more polishing, not less. Other production criteria also apply.
facts.fact: Sake's rice-polishing ratio measures grain weight remaining: daiginjo requires 50% or less, while ginjo requires 60% or less.
facts.hook: In sake, 50% means what's left.

facts.context: Botanicals and fortification do not make it immune to oxidation.
facts.fact: Vermouth is aromatised, fortified wine, which is why an opened bottle deserves different storage from a bottle of gin.
facts.hook: Your vermouth started as wine.

facts.context: An archaeological interpretation; it does not prove beer caused agriculture.
facts.fact: Researchers interpreted residues in roughly 13,000-year-old stone mortars at Raqefet Cave as evidence of cereal-beer brewing.
facts.hook: Brewing before the farm.

facts.context: A mixed fermented beverage, not modern grape wine or a modern cocktail.
facts.fact: Chemical evidence from Jiahu, China, indicates a fermented drink combining rice, honey and fruit in the seventh millennium BCE.
facts.hook: The old recipe was a blend.

facts.context: Evidence at these sites; avoid claiming a final answer to where all winemaking began.
facts.fact: Pottery residues from Georgian sites dated about 6000–5800 BCE provide evidence of early grape wine.
facts.hook: Wine left a trace 8,000 years ago.

facts.context: A museum object interpretation; not a claim that all early writing concerned alcohol.
facts.fact: A Mesopotamian tablet from about 3100–3000 BCE records beer distributed to workers as daily rations.
facts.hook: One early spreadsheet tracked beer.

facts.context: A landmark definition, not the first appearance of the word 'cocktail'.
facts.fact: A definition published on 13 May 1806 described a cocktail through spirits, sugar, water and bitters.
facts.hook: The cocktail got a definition in 1806.

facts.context: First American manual; not the world's first written drink recipe.
facts.fact: Jerry Thomas's 1862 How to Mix Drinks is recognised as the first American bartending manual.
facts.hook: The bartender's handbook is older than Prohibition.

facts.context: A surviving recipe, not evidence Franklin invented milk punch.
facts.fact: The Massachusetts Historical Society preserves Benjamin Franklin's milk-punch recipe, sent to James Bowdoin on 11 October 1763.
facts.hook: Franklin kept a punch recipe.

facts.context: Royal Navy practice; not a date when rum production ended.
facts.fact: The Royal Navy's daily rum ration ended on 31 July 1970, remembered as Black Tot Day.
facts.hook: The Navy called last orders in 1970.

facts.context: Historical institutional account; do not attach unverified pirate-health stories.
facts.fact: Royal Collection Trust links naval grog to Admiral Edward Vernon's 1740 order to dilute rum with water.
facts.hook: Grog was a dilution order.

facts.context: Other laws and restrictions existed. Avoid reducing the whole legal system to one sentence.
facts.fact: U.S. national Prohibition ran from 1920 to 1933; the constitutional ban targeted manufacture, sale and transport, rather than private consumption itself.
facts.hook: Prohibition didn't outlaw every private sip.

facts.context: Political and moral imagery, not neutral comparative health evidence.
facts.fact: Hogarth's Gin Lane and Beer Street were published together in 1751, contrasting social ruin with an idealised beer-drinking community.
facts.hook: The beer picture was propaganda too.

facts.context: A historical lease story; not a statement about current property arrangements.
facts.fact: Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease at St James's Gate in 1759.
facts.hook: An optimistic lease.

facts.context: The publisher's origin account; no claim every pub dispute became a record.
facts.fact: Guinness World Records traces its origin to Hugh Beaver's 1951 bird-speed argument; the first record book appeared in 1955.
facts.hook: Pub arguments got their own reference book.

facts.context: Producer account and specification; the complete recipe is not publicly disclosed.
facts.fact: Chartreuse's producer traces its manuscript story to 1605; Green Chartreuse uses a blend of 130 plants, flowers, roots, spices and other botanicals.
facts.hook: The recipe keeps its secrets.

facts.context: A documented brand launch; not a claim that whisky production in India began then.
facts.fact: Amrut launched its Indian single malt in Glasgow in 2004.
facts.hook: Indian single malt made its entrance in Glasgow.

facts.context: The specific competition and edition matter; 'world's best whisky' is too broad.
facts.fact: Indri's Diwali Collector's Edition 2023 won Best in Show, Double Gold at the Whiskies of the World Awards.
facts.hook: Name the award, not the whole world.

facts.context: The 19 December 2007 date shown in this state-wise list is its filing date, not a certificate-issue date.
facts.fact: India's official GI register lists Feni as a registered geographical indication associated with Goa.
facts.hook: Feni has a place on the register.

facts.context: Urrak is seasonal and usually less potent; do not assign every batch one exact ABV.
facts.fact: Goa Tourism describes urrak as the first distillation of cashew fruit and feni as the second or third.
facts.hook: Same fruit. Another distillation.

facts.context: Fresh juice is distinct from the fermented and distilled drinks made downstream.
facts.fact: Fresh cashew juice is called niro in Goa; Goa Tourism identifies March to May as its season.
facts.hook: Before the spirit, there's the juice.

facts.context: A regional flower-to-spirit tradition. The cited descriptions do not establish a single recipe or strength for every mahua drink.
facts.fact: Mahua's flowers, rather than its fruit, are fermented and distilled into traditional spirits. CSIR research documents this in Madhya Pradesh; India's National Portal also describes flower-based drinks in Latehar, Jharkhand.
facts.hook: Flowers in the glass.

facts.context: Tongba also names the vessel; traditions and names vary across Himalayan communities.
facts.fact: ICAR describes Himalayan millet drinks served in a tongba container, topped up with warm water and sipped through a filtering bamboo straw.
facts.hook: Warm water. Fermented millet. A bamboo straw.

facts.context: This identifies a registered geographical origin; it is not a blanket quality grade for all Indian wine.
facts.fact: Nashik Valley Wine is listed as a registered geographical indication associated with Maharashtra in India's official GI register.
facts.hook: Indian wine has an origin label too.

facts.context: Measured liquids before ice and dilution; other house specifications exist.
facts.fact: The IBA Negroni uses 30 ml each of gin, Campari and sweet red vermouth: a 1:1:1 structure.
facts.hook: Three bottles. No fractions.

facts.context: 'Splash' is not a fixed volume, so do not invent a precise Americano ABV.
facts.fact: The IBA Americano pairs 30 ml Campari with 30 ml sweet red vermouth and a splash of soda; it shares two Negroni ingredients but leaves out gin.
facts.hook: The Negroni's lighter cousin.

facts.context: Before ice and dilution; the IBA notes alternative bitter liqueurs.
facts.fact: The IBA Aperol Spritz uses 90 ml Prosecco, 60 ml Aperol and 30 ml soda: 3:2:1.
facts.hook: The Spritz has a simple rhythm.

facts.context: One official specification, not the only valid recipe.
facts.fact: The IBA Margarita specifies 50 ml tequila, 20 ml triple sec and 15 ml fresh lime juice.
facts.hook: A Margarita isn't always three equal parts.

facts.context: Measured liquids before ice and dilution.
facts.fact: The IBA Cosmopolitan uses 40 ml citron vodka, 15 ml Cointreau, 15 ml lime juice and 30 ml cranberry juice.
facts.hook: The Cosmo has more cranberry than lime.

facts.context: The classic specification is not a frozen fruit drink; spoon mass is not specified here.
facts.fact: The IBA Daiquiri contains 60 ml white Cuban rum, 20 ml lime juice and two barspoons of superfine sugar.
facts.hook: The Daiquiri can travel light.

facts.context: Their ingredients differ: bourbon/amaro/Aperol/lemon versus mezcal/Yellow Chartreuse/Aperol/lime.
facts.fact: The IBA Paper Plane uses four equal 30 ml measures; the Naked and Famous uses four equal 22.5 ml measures.
facts.hook: Different bottles. The same four-way split.

facts.context: No separately added sugar syrup in this specification; the liqueur still contains sugar.
facts.fact: The IBA Hemingway Special combines 60 ml rum, 40 ml grapefruit juice, 15 ml maraschino liqueur and 15 ml lime juice.
facts.hook: Hemingway takes a different detour.

facts.context: The creator's company's account; modern versions vary.
facts.fact: Trader Vic's 1944 creation account lists Jamaican rum, lime, orange curaçao, rock-candy syrup and orgeat, without pineapple or orange juice.
facts.hook: The original Mai Tai skipped pineapple.

facts.context: State this as the hotel's historical account, rather than an uncontested archival proof.
facts.fact: Raffles credits bartender Ngiam Tong Boon with creating the Singapore Sling at its Long Bar in 1915.
facts.hook: A hotel bar wrote a national signature.

facts.context: LCBO notes earlier vodka–tomato–clam drinks; Chell popularised this version.
facts.fact: LCBO credits Walter Chell's 1969 Caesar with drawing inspiration from spaghetti alle vongole: tomato and clam flavours became a cocktail.
facts.hook: The Caesar has a pasta connection.

facts.context: Creator-venue attribution; not a historical Mexican folk recipe.
facts.fact: Phil Ward's Oaxaca Old-Fashioned, created at Death & Co in 2007, splits its base between tequila and mezcal.
facts.hook: The Old Fashioned crossed the border.

facts.context: A cocktail name and recipe history; no medical benefit implied.
facts.fact: Difford's credits Sam Ross with the Penicillin at Milk & Honey, New York, in 2005: whisky, ginger, honey and lemon, with smoky whisky as an accent.
facts.hook: The Penicillin is a modern prescription.

facts.context: Use 'dated by Difford's' for the origin year; recipes and naming evolved.
facts.fact: Difford's dates Dick Bradsell's Espresso Martini to London in 1983; its familiar name does not mean the drink contains vermouth.
facts.hook: The Espresso Martini is younger than it looks.

facts.context: A documented screen appearance, not a claim that the film invented or popularised it by a measurable amount.
facts.fact: The French 75 appears in Casablanca, released in 1942.
facts.hook: Casablanca had a French 75 tab.

facts.context: On-screen association; avoid unsupported post-film sales-growth claims.
facts.fact: The White Russian is Jeffrey Lebowski's recurring drink in The Big Lebowski, released in 1998.
facts.hook: The Dude's usual.

facts.context: Scene description, not a recommended piece of bar equipment.
facts.fact: In Some Like It Hot (1959), the train-party Manhattan is mixed in a hot-water bottle.
facts.hook: The hot-water bottle was the shaker.

facts.context: A garnish comparison, not a claim that every Gibson uses one fixed ratio.
facts.fact: A Gibson appears in North by Northwest (1959); its pickled-onion garnish distinguishes it from the familiar olive-or-twist Martini presentation.
facts.hook: One onion changes the scene.

facts.context: Literary and film references; they do not establish either drink's origin.
facts.fact: Mint Juleps and Gin Rickeys appear in The Great Gatsby's world, from Fitzgerald's 1925 novel to the 2013 film adaptation.
facts.hook: Gatsby's summer had a bar menu.

facts.context: Cultural association, not a quantified causal sales claim.
facts.fact: The Cosmopolitan is closely associated with Sex and the City.
facts.hook: Carrie's other accessory.

facts.context: The literary drink predates the 2006 film. Keep the novel and film versions distinct when illustrating the scene.
facts.fact: Bond's Vesper appears in Casino Royale, first published in 1953, and is named for Vesper Lynd.
facts.hook: The Vesper was on the page first.

facts.context: A reported literary anecdote; don't turn it into an objective judgement of today's Vesper recipes.
facts.fact: An estate-published account reports that Fleming disliked the Vesper when he eventually tasted the cocktail he had invented.
facts.hook: Even the author had second thoughts.

facts.context: A content-analysis estimate about fiction, not measured consumption or a target to imitate.
facts.fact: A 2013 BMJ analysis of Fleming novels estimated Bond's intake at 92 UK alcohol units per week, excluding days he could not drink.
facts.hook: Bond's expense account got audited.

facts.context: The songwriter's own recollection; no song lyrics need to be reproduced.
facts.fact: Rupert Holmes said in an interview that he had never tasted a Piña Colada when he wrote the famous song's drink reference.
facts.hook: The Piña Colada song came first.

facts.context: The count belongs to the inscription description, not a live 2026 inventory.
facts.fact: Belgium's beer culture was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016; its inscription describes almost 1,500 beer types and varied fermentation methods.
facts.hook: Belgian beer is a living tradition.

facts.context: Koji mould and yeast perform different jobs.
facts.fact: Koji helps convert rice starch into fermentable sugars; yeast then produces alcohol. Japan's traditional koji-based sake-making knowledge received UNESCO recognition in 2024.
facts.hook: Sake needs more than yeast.

facts.context: The 2013 inscription describes a traditional process; individual wines and maceration regimes vary.
facts.fact: UNESCO's Georgian qvevri tradition uses egg-shaped earthenware vessels buried in the ground; its description includes five to six months of fermentation.
facts.hook: Some cellars are buried pots.

facts.context: A World Heritage property; this is not the full legal tequila appellation area.
facts.fact: UNESCO's Agave Landscape and Ancient Industrial Facilities of Tequila covers 34,658 hectares and was inscribed in 2006.
facts.hook: Tequila has a landscape-sized footprint.

facts.context: A certification model, not one particular flavour or beer style.
facts.fact: The Authentic Trappist Product criteria require production near the abbey, monastic supervision, and profits supporting the community, solidarity or charitable work.
facts.hook: Trappist is about who makes it, too.

facts.context: A dynamic ageing method; a solera's founding date is not the age of every drop.
facts.fact: Sherry's criaderas-and-solera system blends wine across ageing stages: wine withdrawn from the oldest scale is replenished from younger scales.
facts.hook: A solera is a moving blend.

facts.context: A deliberate production process; not a rule that every film on an opened bottle is harmless.
facts.fact: During biological sherry ageing, flor forms a surface film that protects wine from oxidation while changing its composition and aromas.
facts.hook: This yeast layer is meant to be there.

facts.context: 77% describes the added spirit, not the finished Port's strength.
facts.fact: Port production deliberately interrupts fermentation with certified grape spirit at 77% ABV, preserving some grape sugar.
facts.hook: Port keeps sweetness by stopping the process.

facts.context: These are U.S. measures and examples; larger or stronger servings contain more.
facts.fact: A U.S. standard drink contains about 14 g of pure alcohol: roughly 12 fl oz of 5% beer, 5 fl oz of 12% wine or 1.5 fl oz of 40% spirits.
facts.hook: A glass isn't a unit.

facts.context: A UK unit and a U.S. standard drink are different quantities.
facts.fact: One UK alcohol unit is 10 ml, or about 8 g, of pure alcohol.
facts.hook: A UK unit is a different measure.

facts.context: Our calculation using the NHS formula; not a personal metabolism or safe-driving countdown.
facts.fact: A 750 ml bottle at 13.5% ABV contains approximately 10.1 UK units: 750 × 13.5 ÷ 1,000.
facts.hook: The bottle has more units than glasses.

facts.context: Our volume-based calculation with explicitly assumed bottle strengths; actual brands, ice melt and volume contraction vary.
facts.fact: Example: 30 ml each of 40% gin, 25% Campari and 16% vermouth makes a Negroni at about 27% ABV before dilution; adding 30 ml water gives about 20.3%.
facts.hook: Ice changes the percentage, not the pour.

facts.context: Producer quality guidance, not a universal spoilage deadline.
facts.fact: MARTINI advises refrigerating opened vermouth and describes around a month of good keeping quality before oxidation increasingly dulls its flavour.
facts.hook: Vermouth goes in the fridge.

facts.context: Service guidance; bottle size and starting temperature affect cooling time.
facts.fact: Comité Champagne recommends serving Champagne at 8–10°C and chilling the bottle in a half-water, half-ice bucket about 30 minutes before serving.
facts.hook: Cold. Not frozen out.

facts.context: A practical preservation point, not a promise of indefinite freshness.
facts.fact: Comité Champagne explicitly says a spoon in the bottle neck does not preserve bubbles; use an airtight closure.
facts.hook: The spoon isn't a stopper.

facts.context: Bottle condition can still change; this is about cask-age accounting.
facts.fact: Whisky does not keep maturing in the bottle the way it does in a cask; its age statement does not increase with storage.
facts.hook: A 12-year-old doesn't turn 20 on your shelf.

facts.context: Do not offer a coffee-based recovery or driving-readiness calculator.
facts.fact: NIAAA explains that caffeine may reduce drowsiness but does not undo alcohol's effects on coordination or decision-making.
facts.hook: Coffee can wake you. It can't sober you.

facts.context: A limited study under specified conditions; no order is a demonstrated hangover-prevention trick.
facts.fact: A 2019 randomised crossover trial involving 90 adults found that beer-before-wine versus wine-before-beer did not significantly change hangover severity.
facts.hook: The order didn't rescue the morning.

facts.context: Chemical analysis of a small historical sample, not a clinical test of hallucinations or a claim of safety.
facts.fact: A 2008 analysis of 13 authentic pre-1915 absinthes found total thujone concentrations from 0.5 to 48.3 mg/l, rather than uniformly extreme levels.
facts.hook: Absinthe's legend met a laboratory.

facts.context: Avoid the single-inventor legend and the unsupported 'tasting stars' quotation.
facts.fact: Comité Champagne's history credits Dom Pérignon with improvements in grape quality, blending and winemaking from 1668; Champagne's development involved many people and techniques.
facts.hook: The monk wasn't the whole invention story.

facts.context: A bar experiment about surface water and active shaking, not a universal claim that all ice sizes always dilute identically.
facts.fact: Dave Arnold's experiments found that excess water clinging to crushed ice explained extra initial dilution; drying its surface narrowed the difference from whole ice.
facts.hook: Small ice can bring its own water.

facts.context: Tested with specified ice and 100 ml liquor; texture and appearance were not evaluated.
facts.fact: In Dave Arnold's 2009 tests, cooling largely levelled off after about 10–12 seconds of shaking.
facts.hook: The long shake has diminishing returns.

facts.context: Producer description; the colour is easiest to see with enough light.
facts.fact: Guinness describes Draught's colour as dark ruby red, created by the treatment of its barley, rather than truly black.
facts.hook: That black pint is ruby red.

facts.context: A product-specific technology, not a device in every beer can.
facts.fact: Guinness introduced its widget in 1988; the device releases trapped gas when the can is opened to help create the draught-style surge and head.
facts.hook: The can has a small piece of engineering.

facts.context: A brewing-laboratory contribution with uses far beyond beer.
facts.fact: S. P. L. Sørensen developed the pH scale at Carlsberg Laboratory in 1909.
facts.hook: The pH scale came out of a brewery lab.

facts.context: A brewery laboratory's project account, not a recommendation to drink century-old beer.
facts.fact: Carlsberg reports recovering living yeast from a 133-year-old bottle and using it to recreate beer associated with its original 1883 purified yeast.
facts.hook: The yeast outlived the century.

facts.context: A historical auction result, not today's price or a claim of an unchanged current record.
facts.fact: A Macallan 1926 with a Valerio Adami label sold at Sotheby's on 18 November 2023 for a reported £2,187,500.
facts.hook: One bottle. £2,187,500.

facts.context: The plaque is the small metal disc, not the cork or the entire wire cage.
facts.fact: A collector of the metal plaques from Champagne wire cages is called a placomusophile.
facts.hook: There's a word for keeping the tiny caps.

facts.context: A documented disaster, not a comic drinking record. Conflicting viral estimates of the volume are omitted.
facts.fact: A brewery-vat failure sent beer through London’s St Giles district in October 1814. Eight people died.
facts.hook: London once flooded with beer.

facts.context: This is a statistics story. It is separate from Carlsberg’s pH scale, already covered in F117.
facts.fact: William Sealy Gosset worked at Guinness and published the small-sample method now associated with Student’s t-test under the name “Student” in 1908.
facts.hook: Your statistics have a brewery connection.

facts.context: The official account says “as far as we know” about being the first alcohol brewed there; that absolute first is not asserted here.
facts.fact: In 2011 Barack Obama bought a homebrewing kit for the White House kitchen. The White House published its honey-beer recipes in 2012, using honey from the South Lawn hive.
facts.hook: The White House had a homebrew phase.

facts.context: Mount Vernon documents the labour of six enslaved workers alongside the distillery managers. Published profit figures conflict, so none is used.
facts.fact: George Washington’s Mount Vernon distillery produced nearly 11,000 gallons of whiskey in 1799, using five stills.
facts.hook: Washington had a serious side business.

facts.context: This encouraged an existing trade; it did not invent wine exports or make Henry king in 1152.
facts.fact: Eleanor of Aquitaine’s 1152 marriage to Henry Plantagenet, the future Henry II of England, helped strengthen the English connection to Bordeaux’s wine trade.
facts.hook: A royal wedding helped move the wine.

facts.context: Distinguish the public launch from earlier trial cans. No unsupported claim about being invented in Richmond is needed.
facts.fact: Krueger’s canned beer went on sale in Richmond, Virginia, on 24 January 1935, marking the commercial US debut of beer in cans.
facts.hook: The can was once the experiment.

facts.context: A historical beer-based preparation, not the modern theme-park drink. The cited edition is not claimed to be the first ever; historic pints are not converted to modern millilitres.
facts.fact: A 1594 English cookbook prints a buttered-beer recipe using three pints of beer, five egg yolks, sugar, spices and butter.
facts.hook: Butterbeer had a life before Hogwarts.

facts.context: Tartrate crystals are a normal wine phenomenon. This identifies a specific deposit, not every unknown particle in a bottle.
facts.fact: Wine can deposit crystals of potassium bitartrate, often called wine diamonds. Cold stabilisation is used to reduce this precipitation before bottling.
facts.hook: Those crystals may be wine diamonds.

facts.context: Clear appearance does not establish that a drink is dairy-free or allergen-free. This explains technique, distinct from the Franklin recipe history in F053.
facts.fact: Clarified milk punch deliberately curdles milk, then filters the drink through the curds. Casein binds phenolic compounds, helping produce a clearer, softer-tasting drink.
facts.hook: Milk can be the filter.

facts.context: A controlled sensory finding, not proof that every Bloody Mary tastes better in flight. Noise and cabin pressure are different variables.
facts.fact: A 2015 Cornell study found that loud aircraft-like noise, around 85 decibels, suppressed sweetness while enhancing umami taste perception.
facts.hook: The cabin changes the conversation.

facts.context: A yeast-ancestry claim, not a claim that every beer or every lager uses an identical strain.
facts.fact: The lager-brewing yeast Saccharomyces pastorianus is a hybrid of Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Saccharomyces eubayanus.
facts.hook: Lager’s family tree has two branches.

facts.context: Strain and fermentation conditions matter; this is not a statement that no beer ever contains added fruit or spices.
facts.fact: Yeast fermentation can create banana-like isoamyl acetate and clove-like 4-vinyl guaiacol in wheat beers, without those flavours requiring banana or clove additions.
facts.hook: Banana. Clove. No fruit bowl required.

facts.context: Mixed fermentations can also involve acid-producing bacteria. Brett can form acids under some conditions, so “Brett never produces acid” would also be wrong.
facts.fact: Brettanomyces is a yeast genus, not a bacterium. Its fermentation can produce phenolic, leathery or farmyard-like character; the word “Brett” alone does not specify a beer’s sourness.
facts.hook: Funky and sour are different questions.

facts.context: Liquid volumes are not simply additive. The result is approximate and depends on concentration and temperature; mass is conserved.
facts.fact: In a university chemistry demonstration, mixing 50 ml of water with 50 ml of ethanol produces about 97 ml of mixture, rather than 100 ml.
facts.hook: Fifty plus fifty can be ninety-seven.

facts.context: These are selected requirements of an association labelling standard, alongside ingredient and production rules. Do not present the code as a Japanese national law covering every seller.
facts.fact: The JSLMA standard requires whisky labelled Japanese whisky to mature in Japan for at least three years in wooden casks no larger than 700 litres, and to be bottled in Japan at 40% ABV or higher.
facts.hook: Japanese whisky has an industry checklist.

facts.context: Permission does not mean every Scotch is coloured. Age, cask and natural colour variation also affect appearance; no claim about the share using caramel is made.
facts.fact: Scotch Whisky rules permit plain caramel colouring, E150a, as well as water. A darker colour therefore cannot by itself prove greater age.
facts.hook: Whisky colour is not an age certificate.

facts.context: The historical decree applied to the Duchy of Bavaria. Modern summaries listing malt, hops, water and yeast should not be projected word-for-word onto the 1516 text.
facts.fact: The Bavarian beer decree of 1516 listed barley, hops and water. Yeast was not one of its named ingredients.
facts.hook: The famous four began as three.

facts.context: Dasylirion and Agave are different genera; saying they are unrelated or placing agave among cacti would introduce new errors.
facts.fact: Sotol is distilled from plants of the genus Dasylirion, commonly called desert spoon, rather than from plants of the genus Agave.
facts.hook: Sotol is its own plant story.

facts.context: Fresh cane juice is a useful distinction from many molasses-based rums, but not all rum is made from molasses. The broader aguardente category has different limits.
facts.fact: Brazil’s definition of cachaça specifies a Brazilian spirit distilled from fermented sugar-cane juice at 38–48% ABV, measured at 20°C.
facts.hook: Cachaça starts with fresh cane.

facts.context: The finished drink’s ABV depends on the actual dash volume and all other ingredients. No universal “negligible” threshold is assumed.
facts.fact: Angostura aromatic bitters is listed at 44.7% ABV in its product specification. Using only a few dashes reduces the amount added; it does not make the ingredient alcohol-free.
facts.hook: A dash is still a measure of alcohol.

facts.context: Commercial agave is often propagated clonally and harvested before flowering. “No bats, no tequila” misses those agricultural practices and overstates the dependency.
facts.fact: The Bat Friendly tequila-and-mezcal project asks producers to allow at least 5% of agaves to flower, providing nectar for bats and encouraging pollination.
facts.hook: Leave a little for the night shift.

facts.context: This is the producer’s specific liqueur explanation; colours, sugar and strength can differ across brands.
facts.fact: Senior’s blue Curaçao is flavoured with Laraha orange peel. The producer says its blue food colouring does not change the liqueur’s orange taste.
facts.hook: Blue is the outfit. Orange is the flavour.

facts.context: A producer-attributed origin and ingredient account. Do not infer an Italian origin from the name or apply one market’s current ABV to every bottle.
facts.fact: Kahlúa traces its origin to Veracruz, Mexico, in 1936. Its producer describes combining Arabica coffee with rum spirits.
facts.hook: The coffee liqueur took the scenic route.

facts.context: The microbiology review reports usual strengths around 4–7% alcohol, with variation. Tequila and mezcal use different production pathways; agave is not a cactus.
facts.fact: Pulque is made by fermenting aguamiel, the sweet sap collected from certain agaves. It is not a distilled spirit made from cooked agave hearts.
facts.hook: Agave can ferment without becoming tequila.

facts.context: A film joke and character detail, not an evidence-based mixing instruction. No claim is made that shaking is the only correct way to prepare a Martini.
facts.fact: In The Thin Man (1934), Nick Charles gives a bartender a musical rule for shaking drinks: the Martini gets waltz time.
facts.hook: A Martini, in waltz time.

facts.context: The real pub and the fictional bar have separate histories. A TV trivia prompt should not imply that Sam Malone renamed the real Bull & Finch.
facts.fact: Boston’s Bull & Finch Pub opened in 1969 and inspired the setting of Cheers, which premiered in 1982. The real venue is now Cheers Beacon Hill.
facts.hook: The place existed before the theme tune.

facts.context: The 2009 study examined sales trends and price bands before and after the 2004 film. This is observational market research, not a randomised experiment or a claim about all world wine sales.
facts.fact: Researchers studying US wine sales around Sideways found a stronger boost for Pinot Noir than the corresponding damage to Merlot. The popular story that the film simply killed Merlot is too crude.
facts.hook: One film. Two very different sales stories.

facts.context: A dated supplier history, not a claim about every individual ceremony. Ferrari Trento is a wine producer, separate from the Ferrari racing team.
facts.fact: Ferrari Trento supplied Italian Trentodoc sparkling wine for Formula 1’s podium celebrations in 2021–2024. Moët & Chandon returned as official Champagne supplier in 2025.
facts.hook: The podium bottle is not always Champagne.

facts.context: This is the celebrated deliberate 1967 Le Mans moment. Avoid recasting it as the first time any bottle ever sprayed, or as an F1 victory.
facts.fact: After winning the 1967 24 Hours of Le Mans with A. J. Foyt, Dan Gurney deliberately sprayed the victory Champagne, helping establish the podium-spray tradition.
facts.hook: The spray became part of the ceremony.

facts.context: Rootstock and fruiting grape variety are different parts of a grafted vine. This does not mean that French wine is no longer French, or that every vine worldwide is grafted.
facts.fact: Grafting European grape varieties onto resistant American rootstocks became a major solution to the phylloxera crisis that devastated European vineyards in the nineteenth century.
facts.hook: Europe’s vines needed different roots.

facts.context: A grape-parentage finding, not a blend recipe. Cabernet Sauvignon wine is not made by mixing wines from the two parents.
facts.fact: DNA research published in 1997 identified Cabernet Sauvignon as the offspring of Cabernet Franc and Sauvignon Blanc.
facts.hook: Cabernet has a white-wine parent.

facts.context: The name describes the resulting style and colour, not citrus fruit. Skin-contact duration varies in market usage; the OIV’s formal category has its own requirements.
facts.fact: The orange-wine style is made from white grapes with skin contact: the OIV describes it as white wine with maceration.
facts.hook: Orange wine does not need an orange.

facts.context: This is an important exception to the blanket claim that rosé is never made by mixing red and white wines. Maceration is another Champagne rosé method.
facts.fact: Blended rosé Champagne is made by combining white base wines with red Champagne wine before the second fermentation; Comité Champagne gives a red-wine proportion of 5–20%.
facts.hook: Sometimes rosé really is a blend.

facts.context: Conditions and the state of the grapes determine whether the outcome is desirable. The presence of mould alone is not a quality signal.
facts.fact: Botrytis cinerea is associated both with destructive bunch rot and with the noble rot used in some sweet wines.
facts.hook: The rot can be noble. Or expensive.

facts.context: Madeira can also age by the canteiro method. Do not say every Madeira follows the same heated-tank process or that other wine should be stored hot.
facts.fact: Madeira’s estufagem method heats wine in tanks to roughly 45–50°C for at least three months.
facts.hook: Some wine is meant to take the heat.

facts.context: Large-format names are not uniform across wine regions. Volumes and equivalents come from the Champagne formats sheet; read a bottle’s labelled capacity.
facts.fact: In Champagne usage, a magnum holds 1.5 litres, a Jeroboam 3 litres and a Mathusalem 6 litres: two, four and eight standard 750 ml bottles.
facts.hook: The bottle names need a postcode.

facts.context: An explicitly dated organiser estimate, not a 2026 total or a per-person drinking rate. Do not divide by attendance to imply what each individual drank.
facts.fact: Munich’s preliminary Oktoberfest 2025 closing report put beer consumption at about 6.5 million one-litre Maß, compared with 7 million in 2024.
facts.hook: Sixteen days. About 6.5 million litres.

facts.context: This is the record register’s dated bottle-count entry, not a newly audited 2026 stocktake or a claim about cellar floor area.
facts.fact: Guinness World Records lists Moldova’s Mileștii Mici cellar at 1.5 million bottles, with the record dated 2005; its descriptive text says over 1.5 million.
facts.hook: A cellar counted in millions.

facts.context: This is not the fourth-century Speyer bottle, nor the much older pottery-residue evidence in F049. Nothing here suggests the liquid is drinkable.
facts.fact: A 2024 chemical study identified roughly 2,000-year-old wine preserved as liquid in a Roman funerary urn from Carmona, Spain. The liquid had survived with cremated human remains.
facts.hook: Old wine. Different kind of evidence.

facts.context: The menu establishes the name and price, not a verbatim ingredient formula. The often-told Prohibition-era origin needs that earlier documentary qualification.
facts.fact: A 1916 Detroit Athletic Club menu lists the Last Word at 35 cents, predating US national Prohibition.
facts.hook: The Last Word got in before Prohibition.

facts.context: A comparison of documented recipes, not a claim that every modern Aviation must be a particular shade. The colour is not a reason to replace the violet liqueur with blue Curaçao.
facts.fact: Hugo Ensslin’s 1916 Aviation included crème de violette. The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book printed an Aviation without it.
facts.hook: The Aviation lost its violet for a while.

facts.context: A specification for the revolving bar, not the capacity of the entire lounge. Older Vieux Carré stories at the hotel should not place this 1949 carousel in the 1930s.
facts.fact: Hotel Monteleone’s Carousel Bar opened in 1949. Its 25-seat rotating bar completes one revolution every 15 minutes.
facts.hook: The bar does the turning.

facts.context: That sum measures rum volume, not pure alcohol or a finished-drink ABV. Strengths differ by bottle; the recipe also contains liqueur, juice, syrup, bitters and dilution.
facts.fact: The IBA Zombie calls for 45 ml Jamaican dark rum, 45 ml gold Puerto Rican rum and 30 ml Demerara rum: 120 ml of rum before its other ingredients.
facts.hook: Three rums. One Zombie.

facts.context: Camper English’s experiments demonstrate the method. Boiling water alone is not a universal solution, and a home freezer does not require vacuum-degassing equipment.
facts.fact: Directional freezing makes clearer ice by insulating all but one side of a container, pushing the cloudy portion toward the last area to freeze.
facts.hook: Clear ice is mostly a direction problem.

facts.context: A technique rather than a guarantee of zero residual fat or absence of allergens. It can be used with butter, coconut oil or other fats; no single inventor is asserted.
facts.fact: Fat-washing infuses a spirit with a fat, then chills the mixture so the bulk fat can be separated, leaving transferred flavour compounds in the spirit.
facts.hook: The butter can leave. The flavour can stay.

facts.context: Derived from sugar ÷ total mass. These percentages do not give sugar per millilitre, so a volume-for-volume cocktail substitution needs more information.
facts.fact: Measured by weight, 1:1 sugar-to-water syrup is 50% sugar by mass; 2:1 syrup is 66.7% sugar by mass, before evaporation.
facts.hook: A richer syrup is not twice the sugar.

facts.context: The uprising was connected to colonial controls on basi. The collection contains fourteen paintings; its date is fourteen years after the 1807 revolt.
facts.fact: The Philippines’ Basi Revolt of 1807 is commemorated in a series of fourteen paintings attributed to Esteban Villanueva and dated 1821. Basi is a sugar-cane wine.
facts.hook: A drink became a rebellion’s name.

facts.context: Palm species, collection conditions and local names vary. Neither a universal two-hour fermentation time nor a fixed 5% ABV is assumed.
facts.fact: Fresh, unfermented palm sap is called neera in Indian coconut research; fermented sap is toddy. Keeping sap chilled helps preserve it before fermentation.
facts.hook: Palm sap has two possible evenings.

facts.context: Fining is a production step; this does not imply visible fish or egg in the finished glass. A wine’s vegan status requires production information, not just its grape ingredients.
facts.fact: Some wines are fined with animal-derived processing aids such as egg white, milk casein, gelatin or fish-derived isinglass. Other wines use alternatives such as bentonite.
facts.hook: Grapes do not settle the vegan question.

facts.context: A US labelling threshold, not a global rule or a diagnosis of what causes a particular person’s headache. Fermentation can produce sulfites without an addition.
facts.fact: For wine labels regulated by the US TTB, a sulfite declaration is required at 10 or more parts per million, measured as total sulfur dioxide. “No sulfites added” does not mean no naturally occurring sulfites.
facts.hook: Contains sulfites is a threshold, too.
